newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Rockets hit Kabul as fighting nears.
newsitem.headline: Rockets hit Kabul as fighting nears.

text.p: Several rockets hit Kabul on Sunday as the forces of ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood neared the Afghan capital, witnesses said.
The rockets were the first to hit Kabul since the purist Islamic Taleban militia pushed Masood out of the capital three weeks ago.
Masood, advancing on the city after launching a major counter-attack with the backing of northern Uzbek chief Abdul rashid Dostum, was within 20 km (12 miles) of the city on Sunday morning.
Reporters with Masood's advance force said it pushed a few km (miles) south on Sunday morning to the town of Hussein Kot on the main road running from Kabul to the north.
The Taleban, a mainly ethnic Pashtun militia that took the capital three weeks ago, peppered Masood's men with mortar, artillery and rocket fire.
Masood's mostly ethnic Tajiks replied with fire from multiple rocket launchers as reinforcements streamed down the road.

"God willing, we will be in Kabul today or tomorrow," Masood commander Gul Haidar said in Hussein Kot, about 15 km (eight miles) from the lip of the Kabul valley. The northern edge of the city lies another five km (three miles) down the hill.
Haidar said the forces of northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum were to advance along a parallel route, known as the new road, towards the city.
"They will advance along the new road," he said.
Dostum sent troops, tanks and artillery to join Masood's front line last week, cementing a new military alliance between one-time allies who later turned enemy.

With backing from Dostum, Masood's men made a major breakthrough on Friday, taking Bagram airbase some 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul on the new road and the market town of Qarabagh on the main road.
Since then, Masood has pushed another 25 km (16 miles) south and there are signs of panic among the ultra-conservative Taleban, who have imposed Islam's stern Sharia law on Kabul.
At the top of the pass leading into Kabul on Sunday morning, a Taleban guard at a roadblock pointed his gun at a Taleban pickup truck and told the driver to get back to the fighting.
The vehicle was allowed to drive on to the city when the driver pointed to a wounded fighter in the back.

The guard said he had orders not to let any vehicles into a city, which the Taleban have vowed to defend despite appeals from Masood to spare Kabul yet another of the bloodbaths which have wreaked havoc on the capital over the past four years.
Scores of refugees also headed south away from the fighting, taking only what they could carry or pack on a donkey.
Masood's forces advanced from Kalikan, which they attacked on Saturday night, to nearby Hussein Kot after heavy fighting.
Just two hours before they arrived in Hussein Kot, reporters travelling from Kabul watched huge clouds of dust climb into the wintry sky around Kalikan as the Taleban poured in heavy fire.
Masood spokesman Mirabuddin Astana told reporters his forces were 30 km (18 miles) from Kabul on the new road which leads from the city to Bagram, then swings west to join the main road.
Villagers just behind the front lines said they were eager for Masood to take over the area.

"We are absolutely fed up of the Taleban. If Masood would give us some help, we would fight them," said one grey-bearded old man who said his family was getting ready to leave as the war inched closer to their farm.
He alleged that on Friday, the Moslem day of rest, the Taleban had summoned people in the area to the mosque, where they said an announcement would be made.
"They locked the doors and started beating people. Some they took away and locked them up in a container. When our mullah (Islamic priest) went to ask why, they beat him too," he said.
The people were released in the afternoon after several hours detention resulting from a Taleban belief that they were Masood supporters," the old man added.
